result.summary: Thetis brings Vulcan's armour to Achilles, who ends his anger and is reconciled with Agamemnon, who blames Folly sent by Jove and swears he never touched Briseis. Achilles refuses food and mourns Patroclus until Minerva feeds him with nectar. He arms and drives out to battle, and his horse Xanthus foretells his death.

scenes.title: Thetis brings the armour
scenes.summary: Thetis brings Vulcan's armour to the grieving Achilles, promises to preserve Patroclus's body, and tells him to end his anger.
scenes.stakes: Achilles fears Patroclus's body will rot and be disfigured by flies.

scenes.title: Assembly and Agamemnon's excuse
scenes.summary: Achilles calls the assembly and renounces his anger. Agamemnon blames Jove, Fate and Folly for the quarrel.
scenes.stakes: Agamemnon's honour and the unity of the army are at stake.

scenes.title: The tale of Folly and Hercules
scenes.summary: Agamemnon tells how Juno tricked Jove into giving Eurystheus rule over Hercules, and how Jove flung Folly from heaven.
scenes.stakes: Jove is tricked into an oath that makes Hercules serve Eurystheus.

scenes.title: Gifts, oath and the boar
scenes.summary: Agamemnon offers amends. Ulysses insists the men eat. Gifts and Briseis are brought, and Agamemnon swears his oath and the boar is sacrificed.
scenes.stakes: Reconciliation of the army's leaders, and Agamemnon's oath, risk divine vengeance if false.

scenes.title: Mourning and Minerva's gift
scenes.summary: Briseis laments Patroclus. Achilles refuses food and mourns. Jove sends Minerva to strengthen him with nectar and ambrosia.
scenes.stakes: Achilles is consumed by grief and risks weakness from fasting.

scenes.title: Achilles arms and rides out
scenes.summary: The host arms and Achilles dons the armour. Xanthus, given speech, foretells his death, and Achilles drives to the front.
scenes.stakes: Achilles's own death, which is foretold to be near.

notable_quotes.reason: Agamemnon blames Folly, a divine force, for human blindness.
Achilles accepts his foretold death and fights on regardless.
Ulysses says a king may admit wrong without disgrace.

analysis.text: Achilles turns from anger to grief-driven vengeance. His refusal to eat shows that he is still ruled by mourning rather than reason.
Agamemnon's speech on Folly shows the Homeric view that human error is shaped by divine forces, and that excuse is not full responsibility.
The oath sacrifice and gift-giving show the heroic code of honour in which public restitution repairs a slight.

legacy.text: Agamemnon's account of Folly (Ate) became a classic image of divinely sent delusion in Greek literature.

fun_facts.text: Xanthus's prophecy is one of the few times an animal speaks in Homer, and the Erinyes silence him.

language_notes.text: "Dawn in robe of saffron" is a fixed Homeric description of the dawn goddess, whose robe is the yellow-orange of sunrise; saffron is a crocus-derived dye.
"The armour that the god had given her" refers to the new armour Vulcan forged at Thetis's request, since Hector had stripped Achilles' old armour from Patroclus.
"Grieve as we may we must let this man lie" means that however much we mourn, we must accept his death and stop clinging to the body.
"Meet" means fitting or suitable; the armour is fit work for an immortal craftsman.
"Unsay your anger" means renounce or give up the wrath he has held against Agamemnon.
"With might and main" is an idiom meaning with all one's strength.
"Sons of Mars" means warriors, men devoted to battle, not literal children of the war god. The son of Tydeus is Diomed.
Diana's arrow was the traditional cause of sudden death for women. Achilles wishes Briseis had died when he captured her at Lyrnessus.
"Bitten dust" means fallen dead in battle, biting the ground as they died.
"Ween" is archaic for "think" or "suppose".
"Meed" means a prize or reward; here it is Briseis, the war prize Agamemnon took.
Erinys is a Fury, a goddess who punishes wrongs and drives men to ruinous acts. Agamemnon names her to shift blame.
"Folly" translates Ate, the goddess of reckless delusion who blinds men to the consequences of their acts.
Ilithuia is Eileithyia, the goddess of childbirth; the plural Ilithuiae (sentence 38) refers to her as several birth-goddesses who help women in labour.
"Fall between the feet of a woman" means to be born that day. Juno words the oath so that it covers any child born, not only Hercules.
"To his much ruing thereafter" means Jove regretted the oath bitterly afterwards.
Folly translates Ate, the goddess of rash blindness and delusion, who clouds judgment. Agamemnon blames her for his quarrel with Achilles.
"Baned" means ruined or brought harm to, from the old word bane, meaning destruction.
Agamemnon blames Jove for blinding his judgment (Greek 'Ate', delusion sent by the gods), referring to his earlier quarrel with Achilles and seizure of Briseis.
'Fain' means gladly or eagerly; 'if it so please you' is a polite conditional meaning 'if you prefer'.
Ulysses means that battle yields little: the harvest of war leaves mostly useless straw (dead) and little grain (gain).
'Mourn the dead with their bellies' means fasting as a form of grief; Ulysses rejects it as impractical.
A tripod is a three-legged cauldron or stand, a valued prize and gift. A talent was a measured weight of gold.
The Erinyes (Furies) were spirits of vengeance who punished oath-breakers and wrongdoers.
'Inviolate' means untouched, unharmed; Agamemnon swears he did not sleep with Briseis.
The boar is thrown into the sea after the oath-sacrifice, sealing the oath; it is not eaten.
Briseis is the captive woman Agamemnon took from Achilles, causing the quarrel; he now returns her. Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) is the goddess of beauty.
Achilles killed her husband and sacked Mynes' city (Lyrnessus) before taking her as a war captive; Phthia is Achilles' homeland in Thessaly.
"The jaws of battle" means the fiercest fighting; he will not be consoled until he has thrown himself into it.
Helen's abduction by Paris caused the Trojan War. Neoptolemus is Achilles' son, raised on Scyros, who later joins the war.
"The son of Saturn" is Jove (the Greek Zeus), identified by his father.
Nectar and ambrosia are the food and drink of the gods; they sustain strength and prevent hunger.
"Bossed" shields have raised round studs or knobs at the center, used to deflect blows.
Greaves are armor for the shins; ancle-clasps are fastenings at the ankle that hold them on.
"Redoubtable" means formidable, inspiring fear.
"Fraught with the death of heroes" means loaded with, or bringing, death to heroes.
Hyperion is a sun-god, here a title for the sun itself; Achilles shines like the sun.
The god whom Leto bore is Apollo, who struck Patroclus and stripped his armor before Hector killed him.
The Erinyes (Furies) are avenging spirits who enforce the natural order; they silence the unnatural speech of the horse.

context_notes.text: Oceanus was imagined as a great river encircling the world, from which the sun and dawn rose each day.
The Myrmidons are Achilles' soldiers from Phthia, who followed him to Troy.
Thetis is a sea goddess, so she can use divine food to keep a mortal body from decaying.
Ambrosia and nectar are the food and drink of the gods, and they confer or preserve immortality.
Normally non-combatants such as helmsmen and stewards had no reason to attend assemblies; their attendance shows how momentous Achilles' return is.
Agamemnon was wounded by Coon in Book 11, which is why he arrives last and injured.
Hercules, the Greek Heracles, was Jove's son by the mortal Alcmena. Juno, Jove's wife, hated him because he was her husband's illegitimate child.
Argos was the city of Sthenelus' family. His wife was pregnant with Eurystheus, who was a descendant of Perseus, himself a son of Jove.
Eurystheus imposed the twelve labours on Hercules, a service Hercules owed because Eurystheus had been born first and so held the rule.
Ulysses is the shrewd Achaean leader and the envoy who earlier carried Agamemnon's offer of gifts to Achilles.
Talthybius is Agamemnon's herald, who handles sacrificial duties and carries messages.
Patroclus, Achilles' dearest friend, was killed by Hector while wearing Achilles' armor. Achilles' grief drives his return to battle.
Heralds like Talthybius had loud, trained voices and served at assemblies and ceremonies.
The presents are the gifts Agamemnon offered as reconciliation for the quarrel, now delivered to Achilles' camp.
Peleus is Achilles' aged father. Achilles had assumed he alone would die at Troy and Patroclus would carry home news and his son.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) was Achilles' divine supporter and a goddess of war and wisdom, so Jove's rebuke is fitting.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus), god of the forge, made new armor at the request of Thetis after Patroclus died wearing Achilles' original armor.
Chiron, the wise centaur, gave this ash spear to Peleus, Achilles' father, at his wedding. Only Achilles can wield it.
Xanthus is one of the immortal horses given to Peleus. Juno (the Greek Hera) lets him speak here.

literary_notes.text: Dawn's saffron robe is a stock Homeric epithet that gives the scene a formal, epic tone.
The armour's ringing sound makes its divine craftsmanship felt through hearing and prepares for its effect on the watchers.
The Myrmidons' fear is set against Achilles' gladness, showing how the armour inflames his battle fury.
Even as he prepares for war, Achilles worries about Patroclus's corpse, showing his deep grief and loyalty.
"Silver-footed" is Thetis's regular epithet, reminding us of her divine, sea-nymph nature.
Necessity is described as a teacher who has schooled anger, presenting circumstance as a stern instructor.
Agamemnon deflects responsibility onto divine forces, showing his reluctance to admit fault.
Folly is imagined as a delicate figure hovering over men's heads, tripping and snaring them, making delusion seem external.
Juno is shown as crafty and manipulative; she provokes Jove by suggesting he will break his word, which pushes him into the binding oath.
The remark that Jove would regret his oath hints at the harm that follows, as Hercules is forced to serve Eurystheus.
Jove, the greatest of the gods, is tricked by his wife and cannot undo his own oath, and he can only punish Folly.
Agamemnon compares his own grief with Jove's. By presenting himself as another victim of Folly, he softens his responsibility for the quarrel.
The grim picture of Patroclus' mangled body with feet to the door conveys Achilles' grief and explains his refusal to eat.
Ulysses defines himself by counsel rather than strength, using his age and wisdom to persuade the greater warrior.
War is a harvest, with Jove as steward weighing the yield; straw outweighing grain implies loss exceeds gain.
Achilles turns to address Jove directly, blaming divine will for the blindness that caused the quarrel.
The captive women seem to mourn Patroclus, but they actually weep for their own losses, adding a layer of shared suffering.
Achilles addresses the dead Patroclus directly, recalling his small kindnesses and making the grief personal.
Minerva's swift descent is compared to a screaming falcon on broad wings, conveying speed and predatory power.
The army streaming from the ships is compared to thick snowflakes, conveying overwhelming numbers and cold, glittering menace.
Gnashing teeth and fiery eyes show Achilles' grief turned to rage, now driving him.
The shield's glow is likened to a mountain fire seen by storm-tossed sailors, suggesting a distant, awe-inspiring and slightly ominous light.
Armor that seems like wings suggests Achilles is lifted and made nearly superhuman by it.
Xanthus's prophecy announces Achilles' coming death, adding tragic weight to his return to battle.
Achilles already knows his fate and chooses to fight anyway. This defines his heroic resolve.
